consensus_summary: Egypt is the stable Christian typological symbol of bondage/slavery to sin and the world-system opposed to God, from which God delivers his people, grounded in the Exodus and reinforced by Rev 11:8 and related texts; refuge, false trust, and eschatological blessing are secondary alternatives.
book_summary: Egypt is the spiritual name Revelation gives to the great city where the Lord was crucified, i.e., Jerusalem as a covenant city in bondage under worldly rule and covenant corruption.
consensus_core_identification: bondage/slavery to sin and the world-system
book_core_identification: Jerusalem (covenant city) in bondage and covenant corruption
boundary_disagreement: Consensus extends Egypt primarily to the generic unredeemed world/sin condition (and secondarily to refuge, false alliances, etc.); the book restricts the spiritual designation to Jerusalem specifically and does not treat generic world/sin as the core referent.
material_contradiction: The consensus primary referent (the world/sin-system left in the Exodus typology) and the book’s primary referent (Jerusalem as the city spiritually named Egypt) cannot both be the core identification of the same symbol in the same sense; adopting the book replaces the consensus core.
rationale: Minimum cores differ in referent: consensus = bondage/world-system; book = Jerusalem in covenant bondage. Rev 11:8 as a cipher for apostate Jerusalem appears only as a minority alternative in the consensus and is explicitly framed there as instead of generic world/sin; the book makes that minority reading the definition and distinguishes it from the ‘commonly taught’ bondage/world view. This is replacement of the central identification, not mere narrowing of an intact category, hence DIVERGENT with DIFFERENT_REFERENT.
strongest_objection: The NT’s own Exodus typology (1 Cor 10; Heb 11; Hosea 11:1/Matt 2:15) and the overwhelming patristic-to-modern usage fix Egypt as bondage/world; reading Rev 11:8 as simply labeling Jerusalem does not license making Jerusalem the term’s core symbolic meaning.
